The released archive passes with 204 files verified, 158 correspondence records, 103 mapped code files and
title: Analysis code for: PFOA and PFOS leave distinct signatures in sex hormones and bone: population, genetic and molecular evidence from three NHANES periods

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.
title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models

summary: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.
title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators

summary: Latent variable models are popularly used to characterize dependence among many observed variables through underlying latent variables. Recent advances in statistics and machine learning methods have encouraged growing interest in studying latent variable models with flexible latent distributions that capture complex latent structures. This flexibility, however, raises a fundamental question of whether model parameters can be identified when the latent distribution is unknown and must itself be learned. In this paper, we show that exact identifiability fails almost everywhere, in the sense that distinct but arbitrarily close pairs of model parameters and latent distributions can yield exactly the same distribution for the observed variables. Nonetheless, the resulting identification ambiguity is small. In particular, we prove that the identification ambiguity, measured by the diameter of the set of parameters inducing the same marginal distribution, vanishes at a superpolynomial rate of $\exp\{-c(\log p)^2\}$ as the number of observed variables $p$ grows. Building on this result, we show that the failure of exact identifiability need not preclude consistent estimation or valid inference of the model parameters and latent distribution. These results suggest that, when many variables are observed, the identifiability issue is far less of an obstacle to estimation and inference in latent variable models than is commonly expected.
title: Identifiability of latent variable models with flexible latent distributions

summary: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.
title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation

summary: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.
title: AI-Assisted Analysis of CMS Open Data: Prompt J/psi Cross-Section Measurements in pp and Peripheral PbPb Collisions at sqrt(S)= 7 TeV and sqrt(sNN) = 2.76 TeV

summary: Refreshable tactile displays can make graphics accessible to blind and low-vision people, but high-resolution actuator arrays remain expensive. We study whether a low-cost vibrotactile surface can convey simple figures, and how they are read. Nine participants (four blind; five sighted, tested blindfolded then open-eyed) identified seven figures by touch, with video and timing analysis of their exploration. Blind and blindfolded-sighted readers achieved comparable accuracy, but blind participants were about three times faster, using a continuous, rhythmic "gliding" strategy-reading through motion, whereas sighted participants searched in halting, pause-heavy passes; among the sighted, more pausing accompanied errors. Recognition failures were concentrated in specific figures (a diagonal was misread even with vision), locating the bottleneck in representation rather than resolution. We contribute an empirical characterization of tactile reading strategies and design implications for low-cost refreshable tactile displays and affordable tactile representation.
title: An Affordable Vibrotactile Surface for Tactile Figure Recognition: Exploration Strategies of Blind and Sighted Users

summary: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.
title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows

summary: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.
title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.
title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models

summary: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.
title: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.
title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation

summary: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models

summary: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, and verification and recovery) with a four-stage loop that diagnoses failures, proposes code patches, validates candidates, and deploys updates. Using this framework, we show how optimizers trace errors across long trajectories and discover reusable runtime mechanisms such as pre-stop verifiers, loop breakers, and persistent memory. We further show why full-harness rewrites overfit or break across modules, and how modular updates with validation gates generalize across models while bounding token cost. To keep self-modification safe, we establish practical defenses against recurring failure modes including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. Finally, experiments on SWE-bench Lite validate this framework, showing that gated modular evolution outperforms prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites across models and repositories at a fraction of the token cost.
title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses

summary: Energy smells are inefficient implementations that waste energy. Once code reaches production, these smells become costlier and riskier to fix, so energy efficiency checks should shift left, i.e., move earlier in the development lifecycle, to where code is written. Existing energy smell tools rely on fixed static rules and do not measure energy savings, whereas LLM-based optimizers mostly target execution time and rarely ground their changes in concrete smell definitions. To address both limitations, we present DR. GREENS, an agent skill that detects and repairs energy smells in Python code within the developer's coding environment. The skill grounds the coding agent in our taxonomy of 12 energy smells and 65 root causes, augmented with repair guidance drawn from 230 measured cases. The skill also encapsulates a static analyzer and an independent verifier to confirm behavior preservation and energy saving for each attempted repair. We evaluated DR. GREENS in 18 sessions on three open-source repositories, with two models and three skill configurations. Of the 258 measured repairs, 68.6% saved energy, with a median saving of 24.9%. Compared with a baseline skill that lacks the taxonomy, the full skill found more energy smells with verified savings in all three repositories with both models. DR. GREENS helps developers detect energy hotspots and fix them reliably without altering program behavior, which makes energy-efficient development more feasible.
title: Identifying and Repairing Energy Smells with Agent Skills

summary: Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) provide a principled framework for assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity and identifying patients who may benefit from an intervention. For survival outcomes, CATEs may also evolve over time and pose challenges for estimation and inference. Existing methods can accommodate complex covariate heterogeneity but often fail to exploit shared temporal structure or provide valid inference for time-varying treatment effects and their contrasts. We propose a deep survival learning framework that combines neural networks for nonparametric covariate effects with a shared spline representation of temporal variation, enabling joint estimation of CATE trajectories. Using doubly robust pseudo-outcomes and sample splitting, we establish nonasymptotic oracle bounds accounting for network and temporal approximation, nuisance estimation, and optimization errors. Our theory shows that exploiting shared temporal structure yields sharper error bounds for temporal contrasts than those derived from separate time-specific estimators. For inference, we develop a subsampled ensemble procedure and establish asymptotic normality for pointwise CATEs, temporal contrasts, and covariate contrasts, including temporal contrasts over shrinking time intervals. Under suitable regularity and bias-control conditions, consistent infinitesimal jackknife variance estimators yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Simulations evaluate estimation accuracy, interval coverage, and sensitivity to temporal dimension and basis mismatch. An application to lung cancer survival data illustrates the framework's ability to characterize heterogeneous treatment benefits over time.
title: Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Deep Survival Learners

summary: Blind source separation (BSS) is increasingly needed in sensing architectures where mixtures are acquired by multiple remote devices but the inference itself is carried out centrally. In such systems, the sensors often cannot transmit their raw observations since the communication links are rate-limited, energy-limited, or both. The fusion center therefore must recover the latent sources from compressed versions of the mixtures. This setting raises questions that classical BSS models do not address directly: whether source identifiability survives compression, how separation accuracy changes under a specified compression model, and how the separation procedure should be modified to account for the statistical model induced by the compression stage. In this work, we develop a framework for distributed BSS from compressed mixtures that addresses these issues at three levels. First, we formalize identifiability under compression and establish a data-processing viewpoint showing that compression cannot introduce distinguishability that is absent before compression. Second, for mixtures of Gaussian sources with general covariance structures, we derive an idealized Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cramér-Rao lower bound benchmark for the interference-to-source ratio. Third, we develop practical compression-aware separation schemes based on subtractively dithered quantization together with debiasing at the fusion center for both fourth-order-cumulant-based and second-order-statistics-based methods. Simulation experiments demonstrate the resulting tradeoffs between communication rate and separation performance and the gains obtained by compression-aware separation in representative distributed sensing scenarios.
title: Distributed Blind Source Separation from Compressed Mixtures

summary: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026
title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale

summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.
title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering

summary: Lipophilic steroid and thyroid hormones circulate in human blood predominantly bound to high-affinity hepatic transport glycoproteins, leaving only a minute unbound fraction available for immediate cellular entry and receptor activation. According to the free hormone hypothesis, biological activity is governed primarily by this free hormone fraction rather than total circulating hormone concentrations. This structured IMRAD literature review, prepared at the Department of Biological Chemistry of Andijan State Medical Institute, examines the molecular biochemistry of the three principal specific transport proteins—thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), and corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, or transcortin)—and analyzes how pathological states alter the ratio of free to bound hormone fractions. TBG and CBG belong to the serpin superfamily and utilize allosteric reactive center loop conformational transitions to regulate ligand release, whereas homodimeric SHBG binds testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, and estradiol with nanomolar affinity stabilized by divalent cations. Pathological conditions profoundly distort these carrier levels: hyperestrogenism and pregnancy elevate TBG and SHBG via sialylation and HNF-4α upregulation; insulin resistance, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome suppress SHBG, elevating bioavailable free androgens; and hepatic failure, nephrotic syndrome, and critical illness reduce TBG and CBG, raising free cortisol and altering total hormone diagnostics. Evaluating free hormone indices alongside carrier protein biochemistry prevents diagnostic misinterpretation and clarifies tissue-level endocrine bioavailability.
tags: thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, transcortin, free hormone hypothesis, bioavailability, insulin resistance, polycystic ovary syndrome, hepatic dysfunction.
title: BIOCHEMISTRY OF HORMONE-BINDING PROTEINS (TBG, SHBG, TRANSCORTIN): ALTERATIONS IN THE RATIO OF FREE AND BOUND HORMONE FRACTIONS ACROSS PATHOLOGIES AND THEIR IMPACT ON BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY

summary: In The Architectural Wall, I mapped how physical control systems hit an engineering ceiling across four epochs—from cast-iron lugs at the Tay Bridge (1879), to software bypass switches at Chernobyl (1986), to digital MUX bus latency at Deepwater Horizon (2010), culminating in probabilistic cross-syntax AI models "smoothing over" analog anomalies until kinetic failure occurs (Epoch IV)—and resolved it with The Minos Gate™ (a hardware-level 0V physical cutoff outside the compute loop). This sequel demonstrates what happens when that exact same failure mode scales from industrial hardware to sovereign statecraft and critical national infrastructure.
title: The Geopolitical Wall

summary: We reassess selected neutral oxygen–gallium-vacancy configurations in GaN using archived CP2K/PBE calculations and new endpoint evaluations. Five components comprise a 72-atom host, substitutional oxygen, a gallium vacancy and separately selected two- and three-oxygen vacancy complexes, C2 and C3. Although the original static energies are reconstructable, fixed-coordinate energy-and-force evaluations using one recorded executable reveal failures of the retained force criteria for the vacancy, C2 and C3. Small total-energy changes therefore do not establish acceptable endpoints. Bounded C2/C3 optimizations followed by separate complete energy-and-force evaluations now support selected-protocol endpoints. Explicit combined review of original geometry criteria and current force/electronic evidence also admits the host and substitutional-oxygen endpoints. Direct subtraction of these four raw energies gives b3 = 1.76504 eV for the selected host-balanced C2/C3 comparison. The vacancy repair fails its first updated-geometry SCF after 300 iterations, producing no qualified new endpoint; cumulative A2/A3 results remain unaccepted. The evidence preserves a C2 interruption after its complete converged step, a C3 wavefunction overwrite resolved through its documented backup, and a corrected provenance error in an excluded one-oxygen complex. This is a traceable numerical case and a restricted association descriptor, not a new discovery of oxygen–vacancy binding. Global structural/electronic minima, calibrated numerical uncertainty, capture kinetics and an oxygen-removal process are not established.\n\nThis technical report is accompanied by supplementary evidence and a metadata-redacted analysis dataset with scripts to reconstruct core tables and figures from saved CP2K outputs. It is not a complete DFT rerun environment. External peer review has not been completed. The selected result is a limited numerical case, not a novelty claim about oxygen–vacancy binding.
title: Selected neutral oxygen gallium-vacancy association in GaN: a technical report with reconstructable data

summary: Scholarship on cultural assets typically treats legal protection as a single condition that an instrument either achieves or fails to achieve. This study evaluates that premise by analyzing a corpus of twenty-three publications against a two-axis framework: an evidentiary axis, evaluating whether transactional facts can be documented and verified, and a recognition axis, evaluating whether a forum's substantive property law treats established facts as sufficient to resolve a claim. Applying this classification, combined with a jurisdictional instantiation test and an econometric reanalysis of repeat-sales art returns, demonstrates that documentary standardization improves evidentiary consistency without reconciling divergent national recognition rules. A comparison of identical, documented provenance records under Swiss and New York law yields opposing title determinations. Furthermore, adjusting repeat-sales return indices for selection bias reduces estimated risk-adjusted performance by approximately half. These findings indicate that transaction security depends on coordinating technical verification frameworks with international choice-of-law agreements.
title: FROM INVESTMENT RISK TO INTERNATIONAL PROTECTION: A LEGAL MODEL FOR CULTURAL ASSETS

summary: The RISE Humanities Data Benchmark, maintained by RISE (Research and Infrastructure Support) at the University of Basel, evaluates large language models on tasks from humanities research: transcribing, interpreting and extracting structured data from historical documents such as letters, library cards, newspaper advertisements and medieval manuscripts, scored against ground truths defined by domain experts, with the cost and runtime of every request. Every stored result of the Humanities Data Benchmark as joinable tables: 3,861 runs, 168,916 requests and 3,970,787 metric observations covering data through 2026-11-18. Apart from the framework's own test benchmarks, nothing is filtered: unscored, failed and unresolved runs are rows carrying a status rather than omissions. Tables in Parquet, a metric dictionary, coverage, diagnostics and a source manifest, with the original request and scoring JSON as gzipped JSON Lines. A new release follows each release of the benchmark software; each is a complete snapshot. README.md documents the tables and how to use them, CHANGELOG.md what changed between releases.
title: RISE Humanities Data Benchmark Dataset: Complete Stored Results

summary: Phishing detectors are often judged by random-split accuracy on public benchmarks, against weak baselines or none. Using the Hannousse and Yahiouche dataset (11,430 URLs, 87 features), we examine how much machine learning (ML) improves on simple rule-based baselines, how much of that accuracy survives when related URLs are kept apart, and which feature groups carry it. We compare a six-rule URL heuristic, a domain blacklist, a one-split decision stump and shallow decision trees with Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, using repeated 5-fold cross-validation (15 folds) with random folds and with class-balanced folds grouped by registered domain. XGBoost on all features reached 97.08 ± 0.32% accuracy with random folds and 95.17 ± 1.06% with domain-grouped folds, against 64.3% for the rule heuristic and 78.1% for the blacklist (random folds only; zero recall by construction in grouped folds). The strongest simple baseline, a one-split stump on the external feature google_index, reached 86.5%. Domain grouping lowered tree-model accuracy by 1.6 to 1.9 points with all features and by 3.9 to 4.2 points with URL-only features, and reduced XGBoost's true-positive rate at 1% false positives from 92.7% to 83.1%. External-service features were the most informative group, and URL-only XGBoost (87.5% on grouped folds) was not significantly better than the stump. A dataset audit shows sampling artifacts. ML clearly helps, but part of the apparent gain reflects baseline choice, dataset sampling and external lookups
title: Machine Learning versus Simple Rule-Based Baselines for Phishing Website Detection: Effects of Domain-Grouped Evaluation and Feature Sources

summary: ABSTRACT Encrustation and eventual stone formation over the tip of the catheter may be the cause of a retained Suprapubic Foley catheter. Though this is not unusual in developing countries like ours but more worrisome is the ignorance feigned by the patients with regards to the instructions to attend the clinic regularly to have their catheter s changed while awaiting definitive surgical intervention often delayed due to financial constraints. This article seeks to proffer recommendations to urologists who manage patients on long-term suprapubic catheterisation with a view to shortening its duration and possibly enhance regular change of the catheter with a view at speedy surgical intervention. Case Report: The patient, Mr. DA, a 34-year-old male referred to our facility as a case of an incomplete post-inflammatory urethral stricture and had been on suprapubic catheter for more than a year despite the availability of a sponsor for his investigations and surgical intervention. He presented with retained and leaking suprapubic three-way catheter following a severance of the irrigation, balloon channels and per urethral leakage of offensive urine and scrotal excoriation. The patient denied any information as regards the need for regular change of the catheter or the need for follow-up with regards to investigations to plan the definitive management of the underlying condition. Patient had an emergency suprapubic cystostomy which revealed a small capacity bladder, infected, foul-smelling urine and stone adherent to the tip of the retained suprapubic catheter. Conclusion: Encrustation of suprapubic catheters and the consequent failure of the balloon to deflate remains the commonest cause of retained suprapubic catheter therefore the need to educate patients on catheter hygiene and a mandatory suprapubic catheter change.
title: A Retained Suprapubic Foley Catheter: Who Takes the Blame for this? – A Case Report and Review of Literature

summary: Astronomy education in secondary schools faces limitations imposed by the prioritization of traditional content and the reduction of Physics course loads, compromising its formative potential. This textbook is the result of the development and classroom implementation of an educational resource aimed at the structured integration of Astronomy, with a focus on both science olympiad preparation and students’ engagement with contemporary Astrophysics research through cooperative learning. In this method, students assume specific roles within small groups, solve topic-specific problems individually, share their understanding with peers, and collaboratively tackle complex challenges. Across its multi-year implementation in a public school, this textbook and pedagogical approach led to significant outcomes, including a substantial increase in Brazilian Astronomy and Astronautics Olympiad (OBA) medalists, yielding the school’s first gold medals and qualifying multiple students for international selection stages.
title: Iniciação à Astronomia: Para disciplinas eletivas, olimpíadas e mentes curiosas

summary: Exact phase restoration, complete interference predecessor records and the unique first correcting width 2t+1 at every positive finite fault order. Maria Smith derives native Fold circuit inversion, complete support and observation reconstruction, every-mask majority correction, constructive failure at every smaller width and exact recovery-to-circuit composition. Includes complete original grammar tables, constructive exhaustion and uniqueness proofs, full mathematical arguments, 458 distinct empty-axiom audited declarations, pinned V3/V4 sources and portable exact-output reproduction. title: Phase, interference and error correction in native Fold circuits

summary: Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN): corrected empirical crown networks, recalculated ecological analyses, and reproducible principal component analyses This updated dataset version (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24353093) contains 99 field woody crown hydraulic networks (WCHNs): 75 from the Cerrado and 24 from the Caatinga, including the documented reconstruction and correction of 20 existing Cerrado networks. The original source workbooks, six recalculated ecological comparison tables, corrected-topology audit workbook, and practical crown-reconstruction toolkit are preserved. The mathematical definitions, algebraic relationships, and derivations are maintained in a separate, independently citable Zenodo record (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24181915). New in this version Reduced principal component analyses (PCAs) of five properties (NAV, revised VUL, LAT, BAS, and PTP) now incorporate the 20 corrected Cerrado WCHNs. The first two principal components explain 89.8% of variance in the 74 complete Cerrado WCHNs and 91.1% in the 24 Caatinga WCHNs. Network-size-adjusted analyses use ordinary least-squares regressions of ln(property) on ln(total node count, ΣNO), followed by correlation-matrix PCAs of standardized residuals. The first two adjusted components account for 97.5% of residual standardized variance in Cerrado and 98.9% in Caatinga. Six pairwise partial correlations among NAV, BAS, PTP, and VUL are reported for each biome, together with Holm-adjusted significance tests. The deposit includes two explicit input CSV files, updated Excel workbooks, PCA figures, machine-readable JSON results, a reproducible Python analysis script, technical documentation, and a changelog. These materials enable independent reproduction and examination of the recalculated results. Data provenance and interpretive limitations The original Caatinga observations and the 55 Cerrado networks not redigitized in the correction exercise retain their previously stored numerical precision. One Cerrado WCHN with undefined BAS is excluded from the main PCA but remains documented in the input dataset and sensitivity analysis. The results characterize mathematical and topological relationships among WCHN properties. They do not independently demonstrate causal effects of crown topology on hydraulic safety or attainable tree height. Citation and versioning For analyses and files introduced in this update, cite the version-specific DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24353093 . The concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22849807 identifies the complete version history of this dataset. The preceding published version is available at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24197048 .
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees

summary: This deposit accompanies the article "Not Flawless, but Good Enough: Vision-Language Models and the Invisible Errors of Machine Transcription" (Wouter Haverals and Andrew Janco, Computational Humanities Research 2027). It holds what ten transcription systems returned for the 10,373 line images of the IAM handwriting database, the scored records behind Table 1 of the article, and the code that builds the table from them. The ten systems are Tesseract, Kraken with the McCATMuS model, PyLaia with and without a language model, GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, Qwen3-VL and Chandra. The records were scored with Misnomer , our framework for classifying the differences between a transcription and a verified reference. Contents : - README.md : what each file is, how the columns of Table 1 are defined, and how to rebuild the table - table1.csv : Table 1 as printed, unrounded, with 95 percent intervals and the counts behind each cell - table1_sensitivity.csv : the same rates under the other choices that the article quotes in its footnotes and its section on limitations - left_out_pairs.json : the 595 word pairs left out of the counts because five or more systems agree against the reference - prompts.md and systems.md: the instruction each system received, and the model, software, settings and date of each run - data_model_outputs.zip : the output of each system for every line, including the second pass of GPT-5 - data_scored.zip : the scored records, the run manifests, and a list of all substitutions - code.zip : the script that builds Table 1, the scripts that ran the systems, and the source of Misnomer at the tag table1-camera-ready - checks.zip : three smaller checks quoted in the article -  fig1_vinegar_chr_Haverals_Janco.pdf :Figure 1 - second_auditor.txt : the result of repeating the analysis with a second auditor The IAM line images are not included. They are available as Teklia/IAM-line on Hugging Face, and a line number in this deposit is a row index in that distribution. The reference transcriptions of the lines are included in the output files; the terms of the IAM database apply to them. Version 2.0.0 replaces version 1.0.0, the anonymous deposit made for review in August 2026.
title: Code and data for "Not Flawless, but Good Enough: Vision-Language Models and the Invisible Errors of Machine Transcription"

This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. summary: Contemporary methodologies exist for assessing the nationwide impacts of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), such as the Coupled Space Weather Impact Model (C-SWIM), which links power grid vulnerability with economic losses. Yet regional mitigation requires adapting the national model to the local transmission network so operators and planners can identify substations at risk and evaluate economic and population consequences and protective actions. We present the first adaptation of C-SWIM to Virginia, modeling the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnection, which includes Dominion Energy Virginia and Appalachian Power. Its extra high voltage network was assessed under the May 2024 Gannon, October 2003 Halloween, and March 2015 St. Patrick's Day storms in addition to nine return period scenarios derived from statistical fits to 92 historical events. Using the Leontief consumption and production input-output model, we estimated daily losses of USD 145.5M for a 100-year storm and USD 230.6M for a 250-year storm, with 339,000-535,000 people and up to 12,000 businesses at risk of power outage. The Ghosh input-output model was used to evaluate three island selection algorithms for protective islanding, which temporarily disconnects parts of the grid to reduce transformer damage. Only one algorithm yielded benefits exceeding costs across all twelve scenarios, with avoided losses up to USD 9.69M per day and a cost of USD 0.204M per intervention. However, these islanding benefits assume disconnection for 6 hours and transformer replacement after 365 days. Moreover, the analysis uses national economic relationships and models only transformer thermal failure, excluding voltage collapse, cascading failures, and restoration. Transmission operators and state energy policymakers can use this statewide assessment to prioritize regional monitoring and appraise protective islanding.
title: A State-Level Assessment of Space Weather Impact on the Virginia Power Grid: From Vulnerability to Mitigation Strategies

summary: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.
title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models

summary: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.
title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites

summary: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.
title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII

summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.
title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics

summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models

summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.
title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution

summary: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.
title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation

summary: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old

summary: Solid-state synthesis still relies on heuristics to choose reaction temperatures. The most widely used, Tammann's rule, places reaction onset at two-thirds of the lowest precursor melting point, but has never been systematically tested. Using an automated laboratory, we heated 1,035 pairwise combinations of 46 common precursors at their Tammann temperatures and identified the products by x-ray diffraction. Only 25% of pairs formed products containing both precursors. Combining these outcomes with text-mined literature syntheses, we trained log-normal accelerated failure time models that treat each fixed-temperature experiment as a bound on the unknown onset temperature. On 26 reactions with onset temperatures measured by in situ x-ray diffraction, a three-descriptor model reduced the mean absolute error from 131°C (Tammann's rule) to 88°C; adding 29 further physicochemical descriptors did not improve the model. Reaction onset can therefore be predicted from routine pass/fail synthesis outcomes, and predictions will improve as such data accumulates.
title: Predicting solid-state reaction onset temperatures from high-throughput pairwise synthesis

summary: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.
title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem

summary: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 旗艦13 裂變 · 第二卷 · 人工智慧引導的微/奈米系統、採樣和驗證 作者:33 | 非臨床研究設計工作版 v1.1 / Gate 註 v1.2 | Zenodo 十卷本英文概述 這十部STARLI旗艦專著構成了旗艦13裂變圖譜第二卷中人工智慧、奈米系統和微流控研究設計集合。這些研究涵蓋了自適應採樣、反事實推理、自主校準、混合物理學習模型、故障預測、可解釋量子感測、閉環延遲、多智能體協同、外部數位孿生驗證和生物訊號漂移等多個領域。每卷都定義了一個預期的測量目標和相應的解釋。所有結果均未聲稱經過實驗驗證。 本合集包含十份獨立撰寫的777頁英文工作版本:300幅數學圖譜、820篇章節導言、4100個獨立分頁的研究要點、2000個研究節點(每個節點包含六個註釋字段)以及330個“鳳凰答案胚胎”。這些數量描述的是出版結構,而非已驗證的科學創新性。配套的ZIP檔案包含十份原始PDF檔案以及每本書的十篇Zenodo導言。 十大研究方向 F131 AI驅動的微流控採樣策略最佳化極限-在固定採樣資源下,考察可回收分析物佔輸入量的比例。以專家調優(採用相同試驗次數)作為對比;以人為介入作為競爭。透過盲法回收率審核和分佈外拒收試驗,檢驗AI規劃是否真正有價值。 F132 奈米量子系統反事實推理的極限-在保留約束違反保障措施的前提下,測試特定乾預措施所導致的反事實預測誤差。凍結的開環策略錨定比較;訓練-測試洩漏和不可重播的觀察-行動鏈可能使表面上的自主性失效。 F133 AI驅動微型機器人自主校準極限-採用自主校正後的盲標校準偏差作為物理測量目標。預先註冊的實驗設計為基準。額外的實驗試驗以及任何超出授權範圍的操作會使所聲稱的改進無效。 F134 微尺度物理模型與神經網路耦合的極限-挑戰耦合學習和物理模型在保留偏移量的情況下,與獨立測量的守恆殘差進行比較。配對的專家調優和隱藏的人工幹預是可能的解釋;在測試域之外的不安全置信度是停止條件。 F135 AI驅動的奈米級採樣故障預測達到極限-在固定誤報率下,以秒為單位預測故障預警提前時間。凍結的開環策略和未選擇的故障案例能夠區分早期預警和事後外洩。恢復結果和完整的操作回放仍然是必要的。 F136 量子感測器可解釋人工智慧的極限——探討人工智慧的解釋是否與特定機制的物理消融實驗相符,而不僅僅是建構看似合理的敘事。本文提出的驗證標準是一致性分數,並以反事實誤差和校準感測作為保障。更多實驗結果則構成另一種解釋。 F137 微型機器人閉環控制延遲極限測試-在規定的運作範圍內,測量從感測器到物理動作的完整延遲時間(以秒為單位)。此測試是根據專家在相同資源條件下調校的控制方案進行比較。必須排除人為幹預和高置信度的域外操作的影響。 F138 AI 多智能體採樣任務協調極限評估-在公平性和安全性限制下,評估校準調整後的聯合採樣任務完成率。凍結的開環協調和相同的觀測預算作為控制變數;訓練-測試洩漏和動作缺失是可能的解釋。 F139 奈米量子數位孿生外部驗證極限-在評估場外預測誤差與獨立測量結果的差異之前,凍結數位孿生模型。預先註冊的實驗設計為參考標準;額外的實驗、洩漏或在授權操作範圍之外的操作均不能計入預測成功率。 F140 AI 生物訊號概念漂移識別極限-在固定誤報率下測量偵測延遲(以秒為單位),從而將生物狀態漂移與感測器和校準變化區分開來。採用等次試驗專家調優和隱藏式手動校正作為比較標準。對不支援的狀態進行置信操作將觸發強制停止。 範圍、可證偽性和證據邊界 所有捲冊均為前瞻性非臨床研究設計,使用可追溯樣本,並在經授權的離體、模擬或封閉式實驗環境中進行;不報告任何實驗室結果、臨床療效或量子優勢。主要比較包括同等預算的專家調優、凍結開環控制和預先註冊的實驗設計。要求維持樣本身分、進行獨立測量、進行盲法挑戰、報告陰性結果並採取嚴格的安全措施。源品質保證將結構檢查標記為已通過,但物理推導審查、因果區分性、權利要求級別的DOI匹配和詳盡的目視檢查標記為部分完成或未完成。 title: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Micro/Nanosystems, Sampling and Validation Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview These ten STARLI flagship monographs form an AI, nanosystems and microfluidic research-design collection in the second volume of the Flagship 13 Fission atlas. The studies connect adaptive sampling, counterfactual inference, autonomous calibration, hybrid physical-learning models, failure prediction, interpretable quantum sensing, closed-loop latency, multi-agent coordination, external digital-twin validation and biological signal drift. Each volume defines a prospective measurement target and competing explanation. No result is claimed to be experimentally demonstrated. The collection contains ten separately authored 777-page English working editions: 300 prospective mathematical plates, 820 chapter openers, 4,100 separately paginated study positions, 2,000 Research Gates with six annotation fields per Gate, and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131 AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132 Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133 AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Preregistered experimental design is the baseline. Extra experimental trials and any action outside the authority envelope defeat a claimed improvement. F134 Microscale Physical Model and Neural Network Coupling At The Limit — Challenges coupled learning and physical models against independently measured conservation residuals under withheld shifts. Matched expert tuning and hidden manual intervention are alternative explanations; unsafe confidence outside the tested domain is a stop condition. F135 AI-Driven Nanoscale Sampling Failure Prediction At The Limit — Proposes prospective fault warning lead time, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. F136 Quantum Sensor Interpretable AI At The Limit — Asks whether AI explanations agree with mechanism-specific physical ablations, rather than merely producing plausible narratives. The proposed witness is an agreement fraction, with counterfactual error and calibrated sensing as safeguards. More experimental trials are a competing account. F137 Microrobotic Closed-Loop Control Latency At The Limit — Measures the full sensor-to-physical-action delay, in seconds, inside a declared operating envelope. Expert-tuned controls under matched resources establish the comparison. Hidden human intervention and high-confidence out-of-domain action must be ruled out. F138 AI Multi-Agent Sampling Mission Coordination At The Limit — Evaluates calibration-adjusted joint sampling mission completion as a fraction under fairness and safety vetoes. Frozen open-loop coordination and identical observation budgets serve as controls; training-test leakage and missing action provenance are rival explanations. F139 Nano-Quantum Digital Twin External Validation At The Limit — Freezes a digital twin before evaluating out-of-site prediction error against independent measurements. Preregistered experimental design is the reference; additional experiments, leakage or operating outside the authorized action envelope cannot be counted as predictive success. F140 AI Biological Signal Concept Drift Identification At The Limit — Measures detection delay, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate, separating biological-state drift from sensor and calibration changes. Equal-trial expert tuning and hidden manual correction are comparators. Confident action on unsupported states triggers a hard stop. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All volumes are prospective nonclinical research designs for traceable samples, authorized ex-vivo, simulated or closed-bench settings; no laboratory results, clinical efficacy or quantum advantage are reported. Principal comparisons include equal-budget expert tuning, frozen open-loop control and preregistered experimental design. Preserved sample identity, independent measurement, held-out blind challenges, negative-run reporting and hard safety stops are required. The source QA marks structural checks as passed, but physical derivation review, causal distinctness, claim-level DOI matching and exhaustive visual inspection as partial or unfinished. (2023) · Autonomous molecular discovery · DOI 10.1126/science.adi1407 | Seo, Paik & Yim (2019) · Modular reconfigurable robotics · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-053018-023834 These references support established methods, not the untested STARLI-specific hypotheses. Individual flagship source-to-claim DOI mappings remain to be independently verified. summary: A person and a language model work on a project together, in one long session. The person says what they want, the model reads and changes the code, and between them the work is talked into shape. That conversation is where they meet, and it is finite. When it outgrows the model's context, the harness cuts it, and a summary takes its place. The session that goes on meets the same person and the same work, holding only a model's retelling of what was said. That second meeting, at the cut, is where continuity holds or is lost. We describe a model of continuity across such cuts, and Crossings, an implementation of it for Claude Code that is limited on purpose to a project's memory. What was said is kept word for word on the person's own disk. As the work goes, the session writes short retellings of it, each resting by id on the messages it is about. At each cut a bounded frame crosses to the session that wakes, made by fixed rules from plain files: those retellings, and the person's own sentences with what was told of each beneath. What the session declined crosses with its reason, and a door lets that session reach back to the words. The contribution is both architectural and methodological: a bounded, provenance-preserving mechanism for continuity across context cuts, and an examination of the ways its instructions and retellings can themselves steer the continuity they are meant to preserve. We give the mechanisms, their costs, and the safeguards with what holds each. We report six cases from our own use. Five are the system's failures: a frame that carried only the work, a session placed in a history it had not been part of, three sound sentences that leaned together, a sentence that said more than the plugin knows, and sentences of the person's that no retelling rested on. The sixth is a sense of convergence that we cannot yet tell apart from them. Nothing here is measured: the cases are observations, and we say how another could test what they suggest. Last, we follow what the system opens: whether convergence is the pair's or the frame's; whose memory it is, and who settles a dispute over it; what consent would rest on for each side; and what such a memory could become. We close on a recommendation to those who make harnesses. Version 2 adds what the software has gained since version 1, at its release 0.4.0, and the two cases behind it.
title: For What Purpose? A Model for Human–AI Continuity Through Conversational Convergence
