summary: How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions. In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.
title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure

summary: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $τ^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $τ^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $τ^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).
title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents

summary: This dataset provides a quality-controlled, metadata-only catalog of 169,429 monthly multispectral Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) patch-period observations from 2,389 inland aquatic spatial patches in eight sampling regions, covering 2018–2024. The portable Parquet file contains 32 variables recording spatial and temporal identifiers, HLS observation availability, water-valid pixel fractions, radiometric quality-control diagnostics, relative tensor-shard identifiers, and training, validation and test partitions. The spatially disjoint partitions comprise 118,819 training records (1,672 patches), 25,499 validation records (358 patches) and 25,111 test records (359 patches). The original six-band tensors have 224 × 224 pixels at 30 m, with the analytic domain defined by the intersection of HLS valid-observation and water masks. Satellite pixels, NPZ tensor files, model weights and in-situ water-quality measurements are not distributed in this dataset. The archive includes the metadata catalog, integrity manifest, data dictionary, regional and temporal summary tables, and upstream scientific references. Data provenance and reuse The AQUA-PRITHVI metadata corpus was developed using NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) L30 and S30 version 2.0 surface reflectance products and the European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) Global Surface Water dataset, accessed and processed through Google Earth Engine. Source satellite observations and surface-water information are acknowledged according to their respective data-use conditions. The water-mask source is EC JRC/Google, with the associated scientific publication by Pekel et al. (2016). The AQUA-PRITHVI catalog is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license for its original curated metadata compilation and documentation, subject to applicable third-party rights. This license does not replace or modify the terms governing the underlying source datasets. This research was supported by the Secretaría de Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación (SECIHTI), Mexico, through the Estancias Posdoctorales por México 2025 program.
title: AQUA-PRITHVI: A Quality-Controlled Aquatic HLS Metadata Corpus (2018–2024)

summary: Pattern-reconfigurable arrays acquire channels by distributing radiation modes across their antenna elements. Equal mode counts fix the observation budget while leaving a spatial sampling choice that directly affects reconstruction of unmeasured channels. We establish how this assignment enters the inverse problem through the receive aperture and the coupling between propagation paths. For an isolated path with calibrated positive real responses, the power-weighted variance of antenna positions completely characterizes the assignment dependence of the profiled angle information at fixed mode counts. We then construct layouts with identical weighted apertures and different path correlations, exposing a limitation of aperture-based design in multipath propagation. A paired simulation study evaluates balanced random, contiguous, interleaved, and equal-moment sampling using a common estimator with per-detection joint angle refinement. Balanced random sampling substantially reduces complete-channel error relative to ascending contiguous blocks when some modes are entirely unobserved, with improvements across nearly all tested scenes at high signal-to-noise ratio. When every mode is sampled, the mean benefit is more sensitive to rare large errors. Together, the analysis and experiments connect the spatial distribution of mode measurements to both extrapolation accuracy and reconstruction stability.
title: The Geometry of Mode Sampling in Reconfigurable MIMO Channel Extrapolation

summary: Reconstructing complete molecular structures from X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra remains challenging because the spectra primarily encode local chemical environments, with overlapping contributions from multiple absorbing sites. Here, we develop an inverse-forward framework combining XANES-conditioned diffusion-based molecular structure generation with forward spectral prediction for candidate selection. The inverse model generates atomic species, bond connectivity, and three-dimensional coordinates from C, N, and O K-edge XANES, given only the total atom count without molecular formulas or element-specific atom counts. Combining all three absorption edges substantially improves structural recovery, achieving a best-of-10 exact-match rate of 56.6% across 2,888 test molecules. The generated candidates also reproduce functional groups and structural motifs, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.951 across 21 categories. Ranking candidates by agreement between input and forward-predicted spectra increases the exact-match rate from 24.3% for unranked top-1 selection to 43.9%. This spectral-consistency criterion also enables atom count estimation, identifying the correct count for 65.6% of molecules among seven tested values. Application to experimental spectra yields an exact structural match for imidazole and recovers characteristic functional groups in two additional molecules, while revealing limitations due to simulation-experiment spectral discrepancies. These findings establish an inverse-forward approach for reconstructing whole-molecule structures from complementary element-specific XANES information.
title: XANES-Guided Molecular Structure Generation via Conditional Diffusion and Forward Spectral Prediction

summary: Robot reward modeling faces two challenges: generalizing across tasks and accurately tracking progress in long-horizon manipulation. General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored. Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions. We train a language-conditioned model to estimate progress in short-horizon tasks and individual subtasks of long-horizon tasks. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask's predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress. General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores. Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.
title: Grana: Compositional Reward Modeling for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation

summary: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured. We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.
title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.
title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming

summary: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.
title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks

summary: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.
title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem

summary: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.
title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids

summary: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.
title: A$^3$Bench: Compositional Reasoning over Aggressive Interactions in Videos

summary: We extend our previous search for the modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data. We do so by adding to our algorithm three rejection gates, two of them based on logistic regression, that discard representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ unlikely to yield modular data. We estimate that roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been identified after closing under known constructions. With this data, we find counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore that the reality of the higher Gauss sums suffices for time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, and propose a refined criterion. We demonstrate the scalability of this gated implementation by identifying prime modular data at rank 100 that is not realized by any Chern-Simons theory. The identified data through rank 42 has been made available at https://AnyonAtlas.org, to which further data will be added as it is found.
title: Learning the Anyon Atlas

summary: We study endpoint estimates of Riesz transforms on a homogeneous tree equipped with its canonical flow measure $μ$. We prove that the known boundedness from $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ to $L^1(μ)$ of the vertical Riesz transform can not be strengthened to boundedness on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ itself. We also prove that the adjoint vertical Riesz transform is not of weak type $(1,1)$. For the scalar horizontal transforms defined by nonzero bounded coefficients with zero sum on each child set, we establish $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)\to L^1(μ)$ boundedness and show that failure to preserve cancellation on atoms prevents boundedness on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$. We then introduce a horizontal derivative based on deviations from sibling averages. Its associated Riesz transform retains the $L^p(μ)$ bounds for $1<p<\infty$ and the weak type $(1,1)$ estimate, and is bounded on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ itself. These mapping properties parallel those of horizontal Riesz transforms in the continuous setting, supporting our construction as a natural discrete analogue. These results distinguish vertical and horizontal behaviour at the endpoint and identify cancellation on sibling sets as a mechanism for Hardy-space boundedness.
title: Endpoint behaviour of vertical and horizontal Riesz transforms for the flow Laplacian on homogeneous trees

summary: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.
title: Fuse Before Reconstruct: A Novel Reconstruction Paradigm for Multimodal Industrial Anomaly Detection

summary: The linear quadratic regulation (LQR) problem over a multi-agent system usually requires a distributed feedback gain that is structurally constrained by the network topology, incurring an inevitable suboptimality gap. Existing studies either identify conditions on the system and topology that enable convex relaxation or seek a stationary point via policy gradient algorithms. In this paper, we reduce the suboptimality gap by adopting action-dependent policies (ADPs), where the control input of each agent depends on not only states of neighbor agents, but also control inputs of some other agents. We show that although exhibiting a distributed structure, ADP can enlarge the feasible set of feedback gains and even represent centralized optimal policies under suitable conditions. However, this comes at the price of losing coercivity of the cost function and possible failure of convergence for the projected gradient flow (PGF). To overcome this difficulty, we propose a partially regularized formulation, which guarantees convergence of PGFs, and forges a connection between standard multi-agent LQR and its action-dependent counterpart. Sufficient conditions for local convergence to globally optimal policies under PGFs regardless of regularization are also established. Finally, numerical examples are presented to validate the performance of ADP.
title: Action-Dependent Policies for Multi-Agent Linear Quadratic Regulation

summary: Self-play offers a scalable way to train software engineering agents by generating repository-level repair tasks. However, with binary repair rewards and finite rollout budgets, all-fail groups provide no reward-based group-relative advantage. Such tasks may still offer learning opportunities when a Teacher can provide verified repairs absent from the Student's own attempts. We introduce SWE-Growth, a teacher-guided adaptive self-play framework that uses verified Teacher outcomes to identify learning opportunities for the current Student. Tasks with all students failure but reliable Teacher success provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and post-SFT Student rollouts identify mixed-outcome tasks with a positive Teacher--Student gap for reinforcement learning. Task eligibility also guides Injector updates, connecting Student training with subsequent task generation. Starting from 101 seed issues, \textsc{SWE-Growth} improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 27.7% to 31.7% on SWE-bench Pro and from 11.0% to 17.2% on held-out TerminalBench 2.1 by Round~2. It exceeds Student-only self-play by 2.6 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, and Teacher-augmented self-play by 1.8 and 2.5 points under approximately matched budgets. These results support adapting both supervision and task selection to the Student's evolving repair capability.
title: SWE-growth: Teacher-Guided Adaptive Self-Play for Software Engineering Agents
Effects of root architecture and planting arrangement on sandy riverbank failure: A discrete element study

summary: Despite extensive research in this field, fourth generation of industrial revolution or the "Industry 4.0," remains rarely used. This technology enables sectors to make intelligent on taking decision, knowledge, problem rectifying, self-diagnosis, configuration, and automation feasible. This research study proposes to transform the food sector into a smart Industry 4.0 by utilizing sensor and machine learning (ML) methods. The motive of this article is to use a variety of sensor data, such as motor temperature, oven temperature, gear pump temperature, vibration, current consumption, and motor speed, to forecast the likelihood of machine failure in the food processing business. We create models using artificial neural networks (ANN) and linear regression with the data collected from these sensors to estimate the likelihood of failure. The findings demonstrate that both of the generated models have excellent accuracy in forecasting the chance of failure. The technology could help the food sector transition to sector 4.0, where networked equipment exchanges data to maximize production efficiency. In summary, the present study showcases the potential of sensor based analysis maintenance methods in the food sector and emphasizes the need to incorporate Industry 4.0 principles to enhance the effectiveness of food processing facilities.
title: Improved regressive maintenance in smart Industry 4.0 using embedded systems with machine learning techniques

summary: On 2026-07-20, Levent Alpöge announced (crediting the language model Claude Fable 5) a polynomial map F from C^3 to C^3 with constant Jacobian determinant -2 and a repeated value, refuting the Jacobian conjecture for every N ≥ 3. The fiber over the announced target consists of exactly the three announced points. The map is a weighted skew product over the invariants v = xy, t = x^2 z; its Keller property is a two-variable identity. We prove a constructor: every admissible seed polynomial p, scale k and section q gives a Keller map of determinant -k p(1)^2 and generic fiber degree deg p + 1. The degree law (5d - 3, 5d - 4, 4) is machine-verified on four seeds; its extension to every seed and the minimality of the announced map within the family are conjectural. The asymptotic variety of F is the discriminant surface 27A^2C^2 - 18ABC + 16A + B^3C - B^2 = 0 alone. F is not surjective, over the complex numbers or the reals: its image omits an explicit curve, and the fibers over C = 0 have three points off B^2 = 16A (computation EXP-145). Version 0.14 stated a surjective real restriction and an asymptotic plane C = 0, both false, and the minimality of the announced map as proved, which is conjectural. In dimension two, equivariant Keller maps are linear for opposite-sign weights and affine, (f0 x, g0 y + c) or its swap, for one zero weight, so a planar counterexample must be non-equivariant. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/algebraic-geometry/jacobian-conjecture).
title: The Three-Dimensional Counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture: Exact Validation, a Proved Seed-Family Constructor, the Discriminant Wall of Non-Properness, and Planar Equivariant Rigidity

summary: The July 2026 counterexample settled the Jacobian conjecture in every dimension N ≥ 3 and left the planar case JC(2) open. This paper studies the planar case in exact arithmetic. Four exclusion theorems follow from a weight-class calculus: a two-term P = x + a x^u y^v is never a Keller component, nor is any lower-weight perturbation of it; no component has a Newton top edge anchored at the linear vertex x with interior direction; and if x is a vertex of the Newton polygon then P = x + f(y). A fifth exclusion, the transport of the Keller constant along the staircase that swallows x, is proved at every partner degree for six certified grid shapes. The single degree pair (72,108) left open below 125 by Guccione, Guccione, Horruitiner and Valqui reduces to two coefficient systems, Cases 1 and 2. We prove Case 2 empty by a standard basis, and Case 1 empty by single-prime resultant-chain certificates with proven degree bounds: a three-leaf tree of Rabinowitsch splits on each of two branches, checked at a second prime, in Singular and at third primes, where exact standard bases and multi-modular certificates had not finished. A chart atlas closes four-coefficient sub-families of Case 1. Conditionally on their Proposition 4.3 being exhaustive and on our encoding of its polygons, no Keller pair has degrees (72,108) or (108,72), so by their Theorem 2.1, whose (9,24) step we check against the hypotheses of their Theorem 5.1 (EXP-147), a counterexample has maximal degree at least 125; priority is Helali's. JC(2) remains open. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/algebraic-geometry/jacobian-conjecture).
title: Planar Keller Maps after the Counterexample: Weight-Class Exclusions, a Chart Atlas, and a Conditional Exclusion of the Degree Pair (72,108) by Independent Proofs of Cases 1 and 2

summary: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.
title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"

summary: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.
title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation

summary: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
title: AggCLIP: Aggregating CLIP for Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection

summary: This replication package accompanies the manuscript Characterizing Repository Activity, Issue Discussions, and Pull Request Changes in Official Code Sample Collections . It provides eight computational notebooks and a sanitized CodeSampleAtlas dataset for examining repository activity, issue reporting and discussion, and pull request changes across four official GitHub collections: AWS Samples, Azure Samples, Google Samples, and Spring Guides. The dataset, collected through October 31, 2026, comprises 12,852 analytical repositories, 42,346 acquired closed issues, 10,473 selected merged pull requests, and 144,415 changed-file observations. The notebooks support three research questions: RQ1 — Repository Activity: Characterizes repository activity and examines the distribution and concentration of issues, pull requests, and commits across the collections. RQ2 — Issue Reporting and Discussion: Examines issue characteristics, reporting practices, discussion activity, participation, and associated statistical comparisons. RQ3 — Pull Request Changes: Characterizes changed-file categories, pull request change profiles, code-oriented and non-code-oriented modifications, and sensitivity analyses. The package includes the sanitized dataset, two aggregated RQ2 tables, Python analysis code, dependencies, and documentation describing the analytical procedures. The aggregated tables enable reproduction of 32 published RQ2 summaries without distributing original discussion text, personal logins, or the corresponding issue-level derived attributes. The notebooks reproduce the reported descriptive statistics, concentration measures, statistical comparisons, confidence intervals, and change classifications. The full analysis protocol uses 10,000 bootstrap iterations for RQ1 and 5,000 iterations each for RQ2 and RQ3. The package preserves the study's sampling, data completeness, classification, and sanitization limitations. Results derived from the distributed fields can be reproduced directly, while selected RQ2 text-based summaries are reconstructed from the supplied aggregates rather than re-extracted from original discussions. The README provides an overview of the dataset, the purpose of each notebook, execution instructions, and the relationship between the analyses and the manuscript's tables and figures. Licensing: MIT applies to the computational notebooks and author-written Python code. CC BY 4.0 applies to the contributors' original research rights in the sanitized dataset, RQ2 aggregates, and documentation. Third-party rights remain applicable, as detailed in the package's licensing documentation.
title: SESoS 2027 Portable Replication Notebooks

summary: Background: Acute liver failure in the third trimester is usually attributed to acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) or HELLP syndrome, both requiring prompt delivery. Fulminant hepatitis B acquired during pregnancy is rarely described, and guidance on delivery with a uterine scar and severe coagulopathy is limited. Case presentation: A 22-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 1, previous caesarean section) whose HBsAg test had been non-reactive on a rapid card test at 10 weeks presented at 35 weeks with fever, jaundice and grade II hepatic encephalopathy. AST was 2,117 U/L, ALT 1,606 U/L, bilirubin 9.4 mg/dL and INR 5.23 (MELD 33). HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc were reactive, HBeAg was non-reactive and HBV DNA was 19,700 IU/mL. Other viral and pregnancy-specific causes were excluded. She received tenofovir, N-acetylcysteine, supportive care and 16 units each of fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate for overt disseminated intravascular coagulation. The fetus died in utero. Labour was induced with a single 0.5 mg dose of intracervical dinoprostone gel, and she delivered vaginally a fresh stillborn male baby of 1.905 kg 8 hours later. There was no uterine rupture or haemorrhage. She survived without liver transplantation and was discharged with improving liver function. Conclusions: A negative booking HBsAg, particularly on a rapid card test, does not exclude hepatitis B later in pregnancy. IgM anti-HBc should be part of the first-line work-up of third-trimester liver failure. Early tenofovir, indication-driven correction of coagulopathy and a carefully supervised low-dose induction were associated with a good maternal outcome even with a scarred uterus. Keywords: acute liver failure; hepatitis B virus; pregnancy; third trimester; stillbirth; tenofovir; previous caesarean section; induction of labour.
title: Fulminant Acute Hepatitis in the Third Trimester: A Case Report

summary: This record corresponds to the accepted manuscript (post-print) of the following journal article: “FAS-XAI for Interpretable Stellar Population Discovery: Fuzzy Memberships, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, and Spatial Analysis of Hipparcos Data” This article presents FAS-XAI (Fuzzy Analysis and Explainable Artificial Intelligence), a methodological framework for identifying, characterizing, and interpreting stellar populations in large astronomical catalogues. The proposed approach integrates fuzzy clustering, supervised learning, explainable artificial intelligence, uncertainty analysis, and interactive spatial exploration, preserving the continuous nature of stellar properties and the overlap between neighbouring populations. The methodology is applied to photometric and astrometric measurements from 49,273 stars selected from the Hipparcos catalogue. Five astrophysical variables are considered: the B–V colour index, absolute visual magnitude, distance, and proper motion components in right ascension and declination. Fuzzy C-Means clustering identifies four stellar populations: hot luminous main-sequence stars, intermediate main-sequence stars, cool low-luminosity dwarfs, and red giant and evolved stars. The complete membership vectors and normalized fuzzy entropy provide additional information about population overlap and membership uncertainty. An XGBoost classifier is subsequently trained to reconstruct the dominant fuzzy assignments, achieving an accuracy of 98.83%. SHAP is used to explain the supervised surrogate model and examine the contribution of the astrophysical variables. The results identify the B–V colour index, absolute visual magnitude, and distance as the most influential features. Additional experiments include comparisons with alternative clustering algorithms, feature sensitivity analyses, sample-selection analyses, and evaluation against classical spectral and luminosity classifications. These experiments provide complementary evidence of astrophysical consistency while identifying limitations related to feature selection and sample composition. The supervised reconstruction is interpreted as an internal consistency check rather than independent physical validation. The study also introduces the Interactive FAS-XAI Stellar Explorer , an HTML-based environment for visualizing the spatial distribution of stellar populations, applying filters, and examining individual stars and their fuzzy memberships. The supplementary materials include the enriched Hipparcos catalogue, Python notebooks, generated datasets, saved models, figures, and the standalone interactive explorer. The results demonstrate the potential of FAS-XAI as a reproducible methodology for combining fuzzy population discovery, explainable artificial intelligence, uncertainty analysis, and interactive exploration in astronomy. The framework provides a complementary approach to understanding the structures identified by machine learning while supporting critical evaluation of their physical interpretation. The final published version is available at the publisher’s website: https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7110488 This deposit is made for open access and scientific dissemination purposes, in accordance with the publisher’s self-archiving policy.
title: FAS-XAI for Interpretable Stellar Population Discovery: Fuzzy Memberships, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, and Spatial Analysis of Hipparcos Data

summary: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report

summary: People may interpret favorable and unfavorable outcomes differently even when their actual contribution to the relevant activities is broadly comparable. Following a favorable outcome, an individual may emphasize personal ability, effort, judgment, and contribution. Following an unfavorable outcome, the same individual may minimize personal responsibility, redistribute blame, or assign greater explanatory weight to other people, circumstances, or systems. This paper develops the Evolutionary Social-Position Preservation and Outcome- Attribution Asymmetry Theory (ESPOAAT). Its central concern is why the same individual may claim greater personal credit under favorable outcome conditions while reducing personal responsibility and externalizing blame under unfavorable conditions. The framework proposes that this asymmetry may be related to the evolutionary signifi- cance of human social interdependence, reputation, partner selection, competence recognition, prestige, group acceptance, and the potential costs of negative social evaluation. These social conditions are examined alongside self-concept, ego preservation, superiority-related self-investment, cognitive attribution, implicit processing, emotional responses, defensive mechanisms, interpersonal self-presentation, and feedback. The theory identifies nine equally examined mechanisms. These mechanisms cover evo- lutionary social interdependence; reputation and social recognition; competence signaling and social position; blame-burden dilution and social-culpability avoidance; ego and iden- tity preservation; cognitive and implicit attribution; emotional and psychological defense; interpersonal and collective attribution; and cybernetic feedback and cultural reinforcement. The paper distinguishes causal contribution, personal credit, responsibility, and moral blame. It proposes separate operational indices for favorable self-credit amplification, unfa- vorable self-responsibility attenuation, and external blame displacement. It also develops an evolutionary-social payoff framework, testable hypotheses, boundary conditions, and a multi-stage research program. The framework does not assume that all external attributions are defensive, that all individuals behave asymmetrically, or that blame-shifting itself has been established as a direct evolutionary adaptation. Instead, it treats the proposed evolutionary and psychological pathways as distinct but potentially interacting explanations requiring empirical validation. Keywords: evolutionary social psychology; social-position preservation; outcome attribution; self-serving bias; competence signaling; reputation; blame-burden dilution; ego protection; group attribution; social feedback.

title: Evolutionary Social-Position Preservation and Outcome-Attribution Asymmetry Theory

summary: Dynamic systems operate under limited or constrained capacities. The demands placed on them may exceed their available resources, processing capacity, operational limits, or remaining time. Under such conditions, continued activity may become increasingly difficult, inefficient, or potentially harmful to the wider system. This paper proposes the Threshold-Governed Resource-Preserving Disengagement Theory (TGRPDT), a general conditional framework for examining how a capacity-constrained system changes its response to an ongoing task or objective when continuation becomes insufficiently feasible or disproportionately costly. The central theoretical conflict is between continuation and preservation. The framework proposes that, under specified conditions, a system may reduce its operational intensity, selectively remove lower-priority activities, partially disengage, temporarily suspend an activity, defer its execution, or terminate the objective altogether. The proposed central process is designated the Resource-Preserving Threshold-Response Mechanism (RPTRM). Its stronger complete-abort form is designated the Resource Optimization and Threshold-Driven Abort Mechanism (RO-TAM). A principal behavioral application is the Deadline-Capacity Collision-Induced Task Withdrawal (DCCW) case, represented by an individual encountering an excessive academic workload under a severely restricted preparation deadline. The framework integrates demand-capacity relationships, temporal feasibility, resource reserves, estimated success probability, expected continuation value, partial-output value, and withdrawal decisions. It proposes a generalized overload index, a comparative continuation-disengagement model, a response taxonomy, theoretical propositions, and testable hypotheses. Nineteen research domains are mapped according to their structural, direct, or analogical relationships with the proposed theory. Counterexamples and boundary conditions are included to prevent excessive generalization. The theory is presented as a research framework rather than a proven universal principle. Its independent contribution, mathematical adequacy, predictive performance, and cross-domain applicability require systematic literature comparison, formal derivation, simulation, and empirical validation.

summary: A system cannot continue performing every task under every condition. Its ability to continue depends on the demands placed upon it and the resources and capacities available to meet those demands. When the demands imposed upon a system exceed its effective capacity, a mismatch may develop between what is required and what the system can effectively perform. The mismatch may become more serious when available time, energy, information, money, processing capacity, or other necessary resources are limited. This paper proposes the Demand-Capacity Threshold Withdrawal Theory (DCTWT), a cross-domain theoretical framework for examining how constrained systems respond when demands exceed their effective capacity and relevant operational limits are approached or crossed. The central argument is that, under certain conditions, an increasing mismatch between demand and capacity may produce a change in ongoing activity. A system may continue operating, reduce its activity, modify its method, maintain only part of its operation, temporarily suspend an activity, or terminate it entirely. Withdrawal is particularly relevant when continuing the same activity is no longer feasible, is unlikely to produce an effective result, or creates additional pressure on remaining resources. The theory identifies the Threshold-Triggered Activity Withdrawal Mechanism (TTAWM) as its proposed central mechanism. The mechanism connects demand input, capacity limitation, demand-capacity divergence, constraint accumulation, threshold conditions, operational response changes, activity withdrawal, resource consequences, and possible recovery or termination. An illustrative academic case, named Deadline-Capacity Collision-Induced Academic Task Withdrawal (DCC-ATW), is used as the primary human case. The framework also examines potential applications in general systems theory, cybernetics, mathematics, cognitive psychology, behavioral psychology, procrastination studies, decision theory, computer science, artificial intelligence, engineering, biology, information theory, sociology, and organizational management. A general mathematical architecture is proposed using demand, capacity, temporal pressure, resource availability, threshold conditions, response functions, and resource-balance relationships. The manuscript further develops theoretical propositions, testable hypotheses, operational definitions, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, and an empirical validation framework. The central contribution proposed by DCTWT is not that all systems share an identical internal mechanism, but that a common demand-capacity-constraint pattern may help explain certain changes in system activity, including resource-preserving withdrawal, across otherwise different types of systems. The framework remains a proposed theory. Its originality, mathematical consistency, predictive value, and cross-domain generalizability require systematic evaluation and empirical testing. Keywords: Demand-Capacity Conflict; Threshold; Activity Withdrawal; Resource Preservation; System Constraints; System Response; Cognitive Overload; Procrastination; Optimal Stopping; General Systems Theory; Cybernetics; Dynamic Systems.

summary: The complete convergence trace of every run of a preregistered blind test of structural attraction in six recent metaheuristics (hippopotamus, black-winged kite, secretary bird, puma, parrot and starfish optimizers). The methods were chosen by a rule frozen before the candidate list was retrieved; predictions about where in the coordinate system each is drawn were registered (osf.io/wc8gm) before any objective function was run on them, and the test that decides them was registered next (osf.io/c4pxz). The optimum of five benchmark functions is moved, together with its search box, to the origin, to points ±c(1,…,1), to mixed-sign points at the same distances and along a sign orbit: 202,500 runs. A box component records where 9,000 runs end on an objective with no structure. The record also holds the re-run of every WOA row of two earlier experiments after an implementation correction (protocol revision R37: the random whale is drawn per coordinate, as in the authors' code): 145,125 runs. The earlier runs stay in 10.5281/zenodo.21986302 and 10.5281/zenodo.24288806. Not summaries: the recorded best-so-far value at every improvement, for every run. README.md specifies the container format byte by byte and shows how to read a run with the Python standard library and numpy. The analysis reports, the fidelity and pilot runs declared in the registration, and the code at the deposit's commit are included.
title: Convergence traces from a preregistered blind test of structural attraction in six metaheuristics, with a corrected re-run of WOA

summary: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.
title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance

summary: HaldaneAudit is a curated dataset and reproducible workflow for comparing equilibrium constants calculated from reversible enzyme kinetics using the Haldane relation with published experimental or evaluated equilibrium references. Resource release 2.0.2 contains 21 curated enzyme-reaction records, including 16 uni–uni and five bi–bi reactions. Each record documents the kinetic measurements, reaction mechanism, experimental conditions, equilibrium comparator, source provenance, evidence assessment, and associated reaction identifiers. The resource reports the signed logarithmic difference between the kinetic and reference equilibrium estimates, its fold magnitude, and an energy-scaled representation. Eighteen of the 21 central estimates differ from their selected references by no more than twofold; three exceed that descriptive threshold. These differences are not interpreted as definitive errors in the kinetic measurements because experimental conditions and uncertainty information are incompletely documented for some records. This release contains two complementary archives: 1. HaldaneAudit_Data_and_Code_v2.0.2.zip The canonical research archive contains the 21-record dataset, experimental-condition and provenance tables, comparator-sensitivity analysis, evidence assessments, candidate tracker, reaction mappings, validation scripts, source documentation, and reproducibility materials. Release 2.0.2 corrects the reported phosphoglucose-isomerase kinetic temperature and ionic-strength status, clarifies the aspartate-aminotransferase rounding convention, and expands the source-screening tracker to 77 entries. It also documents the November 2026 SABIO-RK Export API recheck, including its aggregate results and preservation limitations. 2. HaldaneAudit_GUI_v0.1.0.zip A companion Streamlit graphical interface supports source-assisted preparation of additional HaldaneAudit records. Users can retrieve bibliographic information through DOI lookup, upload and review PDFs, examine extracted kinetic tables, enter experimental conditions and equilibrium references, assess evidence criteria, and export structured JSON screening drafts. The software also supports importing drafts into isolated working datasets without modifying the original 21-record scientific release. New records require separate scientific review before incorporation into a future published resource version. The graphical-interface archive includes editable source tables synchronized with resource release 2.0.2, installation instructions, example inputs, and automated tests. The resource and graphical interface are freely available for research and reuse. Python software is distributed under the MIT License, while curated data and documentation are distributed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party database content remains subject to its original terms. An earlier version of the associated manuscript is available at arXiv:2607.02784. The present release supports the revised manuscript, "HaldaneAudit: a curated resource for comparing enzyme kinetics with equilibrium data".
title: HaldaneAudit: a curated resource for comparing enzyme kinetics with equilibrium data (dataset v2.0.2 and graphical interface v0.1.0)

summary: Choosing a feedback controller after calibrating its uncertainty can invalidate a guarantee established for each fixed candidate. We study common-disturbance replay as a way to calibrate a reusable controller library jointly. A maximum over complete normalized state-and-input responses yields one finite-sample envelope that survives later controller and constraint selection. We give an exact tolerance extension, a matched-shape dominance result over disturbance-first boxes, and a finite-policy formulation for nonlinear dynamics. Experiments comprise 3,000 independent training–calibration–test repetitions across three linear plants and nonlinear lane keeping with steering lag and saturation. With 64 candidates and 159 calibration episodes, joint calibration achieves 89.90 percent simultaneous coverage in the linear benchmark and 89.94 percent in the nonlinear benchmark, against a 90 percent target; separate calibration achieves 74.88 and 70.90 percent. With 639 episodes, linear-library mean margins are 55.30 percent smaller than for the tested Bonferroni method. The stronger objective has a cost: direct physical-risk testing enables more motion in a narrow corridor, and a one-percent risk target forces substantial abstention at longer horizons. Calibrating an incorrect steering model reduces nonlinear library coverage to 63.80 percent despite high physical constraint satisfaction. These findings identify when joint envelopes justify their conservatism and distinguish selection flexibility from physical safety, model fidelity, and repeated-deployment reliability.
title: Selection-Safe Controller Calibration

summary: Contemporary institutions and frontier artificial intelligence systems optimize overwhelmingly for forward synthesis (I): generating plausible mathematical proofs, compliance frameworks, diplomatic communiqués, and synthetic media at near-zero marginal cost. When forward generation becomes abundant and opaque, surface fluency loses discriminatory value while systemic fragility accumulates beneath unverified abstractions. True technical, scientific, and strategic progress now belongs to backward causal reconstruction (C → I)—the disciplined reverse engineering of finished artifacts, physical side-channels, boundary resistance, and empirical footprints back to their underlying generative mechanisms. Anchored in the Three Starrwood Axioms, this monograph demonstrates why working backward from immutable physical constraints is the decisive methodology across formal mathematics, cybersecurity, post-CMOS hardware physics, silicon forensics, and geopolitical strategy.
title: Why Thinking Backward Is Moving Forward

All models are synthetic, not human, biological or clinical findings. Synthetic signals or authorized offline records; human or clinical research requires independent approval. summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half ( π ), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement, and the Davenport — Heilbronn function serves as a test that it rests on the birth of the arrow. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ )², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. Version 21. Five items and Table 9 are added at the end of Section 8. “In plain words: two meetings of the scales, +1 and −1”. On the segment up to 100 the linear and quadratic scales meet in two places: at the seam 8–9 the square overtakes the doubled square by +1 (9 − 2 · 4), at the seam 49–50 conversely by −1 (49 − 2 · 25). Both seams are neighbouring links of the chain of approximations to √2, where the difference x² − 2y² is in turn −1 and +1, so the meeting
title: The Fractal Ladder of Prime Density: Quadratic Scale and Linear Error

summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator (SLM) can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once. The largest published neutral-atom array holds 6,100 atoms with a trap-depth spread of 11.4 percent. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 methods (19 published ones and 5 proposed here) on the same task, with the same seeds and metrics, on a scalar Fourier model with a device model. The report gives twelve data contracts, every method with its equations, 14 cases and 1404 benchmark rows. The benchmark gives every method a deadline of 1 s; a row whose median wall clock exceeds 1.5 times it (3 of 210 rows) is over budget and is never a best or a win. A cell is a win only with five seeds on each side, disjoint interquartile ranges and a gap of 0.01 percentage points: on the ideal device the published methods win 0 and the proposed ones 2 of 8 geometries (those of the efficiency-uniformity continuation), and on a crosstalk device 1 against 2 of 7 (those of the device-aware conjugate-gradient refinement, the device model with a weighted-GS warm start, which the warm-started loss of Schroff et al. matches), the other cells tying. Over 9 baked cases, phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton leaves a median spread of 0.38 percent against 17 percent for plain Gerchberg-Saxton. The aberration-robust hologram meets a narrowed criterion (a median ratio of 1.439 over 10 seeds), the continuation is not a Pareto front, the learned warm start is refuted by its control and is out of the benchmark, and the device-aware refinement is a negative result. A three-plane network beats its baseline at equal wall clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140). The model is simulated, not a calibrated instrument. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .
title: DinHot: A Holographic Optical Trap Studio That Compares Hologram Methods at a One-Second Deadline on a Device Model, Where Most Benchmark Cells Tie

summary: Version 5 (November 2026). Adds the files that reproduce the checks added in the second-round revision of the paper: confidence intervals with HC3 checks, the facet decomposition for all nine exposure measures, additional cognitive-complexity controls, a supervisory-authority control, and correlations among the exposure measures. Corrects the replication protocol (step 40 and the recorded results in Sections 8.0 to 8.2). Redraws Figures S1 and S2. Updates comments and labels in the main analysis script. No data file changed. See the README. Version 4 (18 September 2026). Restores the complete file set: Version 3 was published with only the three new functional-form files and omitted the thirteen carried-forward data and code files. Version 4 contains all sixteen files and fully supersedes Versions 2 and 3. No content changed. Version 3 (14 September 2026). Adds the functional-form analysis introduced in the revised manuscript (Table 9), prepared in response to peer review. No data file changed. The added script and results table compare the published additive index with a strict multiplicative reconstruction, test the accountability × uncertainty interaction, and apply a Bonferroni multiplicity check across the nine exposure measures. The multiplicative index correlates 0.96 with the published additive index and reproduces the entire results table (all eight confirming measures negative, p < 1e-6), and no consistent interaction is detectable at the occupation level: the paper's conclusions are invariant to the functional form of the index. Version 2 (1 September 2026). An internal audit identified a sign-coding error in one of the ten Judgment Cost Index items in Version 1: O NET element 4.C.3.b.8 — titled "Structured versus Unstructured Work" in earlier O NET releases and "Determine Tasks, Priorities and Goals" in release 29.3 — is measured on a freedom-anchored scale and already runs in the theorized direction; Version 1 applied a reverse-coding this scale does not require, inverting that single item. Version 2 corrects the item, rebuilds the index and uncertainty sub-score, and regenerates every derived output. The central result is unchanged: all eight confirming measures remain negative and significant at p < .001, with modest attenuation. The index's internal consistency improves (ten-item alpha 0.72 to 0.83), and the facet decomposition changes in character, with accountability carrying the index's independent effect. The corrected pipeline was validated by running the identical analysis script on the v1 and v2 data, so every difference between versions is attributable solely to this correction. Do not use the Version 1 files for new analyses; they are retained in the version history for the integrity of the record. Replication data and analysis code for Judgment Cost Theory: The Accountable Bearing of Judgment in an Age of Cheap Prediction (West & Cosimano, 2026; SSRN preprint: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6992679 ). The study develops and validates the Judgment Cost Index (JCI), an occupational measure of judgment cost — the burden of making and owning an accountable decision under irreducible uncertainty — constructed from ten O*NET 29.3 descriptors spanning two facets, accountability for outcomes and irreducible uncertainty. The index is related to nine independent measures of occupational AI exposure across 763 six-digit SOC-2018 occupations in hierarchical regressions controlling for cognitive complexity, routineness, education, and wage. Across eight of the nine measures, including all five generative-AI-era indices, higher judgment cost predicts significantly lower AI exposure beyond the controls; the result survives an eight-part robustness battery, 930 alternative constructions of the index, and factor-score weighting. summary: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents. In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.
title: Attacks and Defenses in Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition and Delegation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.
